en: The Ritual Manual for the Recitation of Avalokiteśvara, the Sovereign of Great Compassion with the Blue Neck,
according to the Yoga of the Vajraśekhara,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Vajrabodhi of South India by Imperial Decree, with the scribe being Yi Xing.
I prostrate to the heroic and fierce Honored One Akṣobhya, to Ratnasaṃbhava Tathāgata, Ākāśagarbha, and Avalokiteśvara;
to Dharmadhātu, Dharma, Amoghasiddhi, and Karmavajra;
and to the sixteen deities of the eight inner and outer arches, together with their corresponding guardians of the four gates.
Relying upon the *Vajraśekhara-yoga-sūtra*,
I shall expound the essential Dharma-methods of the Lotus Dharma for the practice of the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvararāja.
One who desires to ascend to the palace, maṇḍala, stūpa, or temple of the Honored Deity [should proceed as follows].
First, by reciting this dhāraṇī, one obtains immeasurable merit.
If one does not recite this dhāraṇī, then whenever one enters a monastery,
a residence, a hall, or a stūpa, [the same result follows].
All previously accumulated merits will be completely worn away and exhausted.
The dhāraṇī is as follows:
Namo samantavajrāṇām | Oṃ vajratuṇḍa hūṃ svāhā. Next, perform the seal for opening the vajra gates.
Then, forming the double-vajra-bind with both hands, recite "HŪṂ HŪṂ HŪṂ" three times.
Like the sound of thunder, this awakens all the Tathāgatas of the Great Lotus Family and the Vajra Family.
Contemplate yourself as being identical to them;
with inner and outer transcendence free from obstruction, focus the mind on a single thought-moment.
Next, open the gates and perform empowerment for each one without hindrance, reciting this mantra: "HŪṂ HŪṂ," with a sound like the roar of thunder.
The visualization and its characteristics have been transmitted through oral lineage.
Generally, those who wish to practice yoga and enter the *samādhi* stage must first enter the consecration *samaya-maṇḍala*.
Having generated the great bodhicitta, they benefit all beings by relinquishing their bodies, lives, and wealth;
with courageous diligence, they remain in constant accord with mindfulness, such that loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity are uninterrupted.
Such a person as this should then practice the methods for drawing mandalas, images, and so forth,
in detail as explained elsewhere.
Whenever one enters a vihāra wishing to practice mindfulness,
one should first prostrate with the five limbs touching the ground to the Honored One, the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvararāja. Next,
one should prostrate to the Tathāgata Amoghasiddhi of the north, and so on, up to the Tathāgatas Akṣobhya, Ratnasambhava, and Vairocana.
All together, according to the Dharma, they prostrate with utmost sincerity and reverence;
kneeling on both knees and joining their palms like lotus buds, they repent for all transgressions of the three karmas.
Recite this mantra, saying:
"From immeasurable kalpas past, I have been submerged in the sea of birth and death;
now, with a pure mind, I confess and repent my transgressions."
Just as all Buddhas have performed confession, so do I now likewise vow that I and all sentient beings shall all be completely purified.

Recite this secret mantra: Oṃ sarvadharmāḥ svabhāvaśuddhāḥ svabhāvaśuddho ’haṃ. Next, one should rejoice in the merit and wisdom accumulated by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the past, present, and future.
The roots of goodness accumulated by the Buddhas of the past, present, and future, as well as by Bodhisattvas and sentient beings—
having joined one's palms, one should rejoice in them all. Next,
one should place the right knee on the ground and, with palms hollowed and joined, place them upon the crown of the head.
Visualize paying homage to the feet of all the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, and Bodhisattvas.
Recite the secret mantra:
Oṃ padma-vī. (The above is the Earth-Holding Seal.)
Having performed prostrations to all the Buddhas with the Vajrarāja-mudrā, one sits upon the seat according to the mudrā and enters meditative absorption.
One contemplates that immeasurable Tathāgatas pervade the entire realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) in common.
The practitioner visualizes their own body as being entirely present within that assembly.
Then, they bind the Secret Samaya Mudrā: join the tips of the six fingers together;

slightly bend the index and middle fingers (the *vīrya* fingers) to press down upon the upper ridges of the ring and little fingers (the *kṣānti* and *praṇidhāna* fingers), while the thumbs (*dhyāna* and *prajñā* fingers) press down upon the lower parts of the index and middle fingers.
Place it upon the crown of the head.
The mantra is:
Oṃ tathāgata-svabhāvāya svāhā. Next, the lotus family samaya-dhāraṇī-mudrā is explained.
Then, with both hands joined in the lotus-anjali gesture,
the thumbs and ring fingers are pressed together,
with the heads of the fingers separated by one inch.
Place it upon the right ear.
The mantra is:
Oṃ padmavajrāya svāhā. Next, bind the seal of the Sarvavajrasamaya-dhāraṇī.
The wisdom of generosity and the wisdom of dhyāna are interlocked in alternation.
First, the seal is formed at the heart;
the "wondrous word" is placed at the left ear and advanced.
Having finished reciting the secret mantra three times,
the wheel is dispersed from the crown.
The secret mantra says:
Oṃ maruḥ svabhāvāya svāhā. Next, bind the seal of the Sarvavajrakāyarakṣā-dhāraṇī:
interlace the fingers of the left hand (precept) and the right hand (generosity) with the tips of the middle fingers (wisdom) inside.
The two fingers of the patience (kṣānti) and vow (praṇidhāna) are raised like a banner.
The application of energy (vīrya) and power (bala) are bent behind the backs of the patience and vow fingers; they extend three parts beyond their backs, forming the shape of a hook.
The mantra is:
Oṃ vajragīte prajñaptaye svāhā. This is the Vajra-flame earth-boundary dhāraṇī mudrā.

By means of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), one enters the interval between the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*) and the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). By means of the perfection of ethical discipline, one enters the interval between the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*) and the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*).
By means of the perfection of aspiration, one enters from behind the back into the interval between the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*) and the perfection of patience.
Through skillful means, they enter between the perfections of giving (dāna) and ethical discipline (śīla);
giving, wisdom, diligence, power, meditation,
and knowledge each touch one another at their heads.
Cover it facing downward.
The *dhyāna* and *prajñā* [fingers] rest upon the ground like the shape of a driven stake.
Recite the mantra three times.
Visualize a single-pronged vajra-flame mallet piercing through to the adamantine limit (*vajraprākāra*). The mantra is:
*Oṃ kili kili vajramāri trimukha bandha bandha hūṃ phaṭ*. This is the mantra and mudrā for the adamantine fire-city, the flying-flame lightning, and the enclosure boundary (*maṇḍalaprākāra*).
Following the previous earth-seal (bhūmimudrā), open the *cena* and *jñāna* fingers.
Rotate to the right eight times while reciting the mantra three times;
[the range] will be as desired, whether far or near.
The mantra is:
Oṃ sarā sarā vajraprakara hūṃ phaṭ. This is the mantra and mudrā for the boundary of the vajra-flame-net.
Also following the previous earth-seal mudrā,
open wide and extend the wisdom-fingers (*jñāna-aṅguli*) straight upward;
bring them over the crown of the head three times.
Recite the mantra three times.
Visualize vajra-flame nets extending upward to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
The secret mantra is as follows:
Oṃ viśvapadma-kṣa-vajrapañjara hūṃ phaṭ. Next, perform the mudrā of the Vajra Flame-Fire Boundary.
The Samādhi and Prajñā [fingers] are placed side by side;
the Dhyāna and Jñāna [fingers] are held upright, three inches apart,
with the tips curling to the right at the top.
Visualize that outside the walls and nets,
flames rise up to the summit.
The mantra says:
Oṃ āsaṃjñāni svāhā. For one who performs this boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*),
the six classes of Māras and all the Vināyakas shall be struck with terror and flee, finding no place to hide.
Next, form the mudrā of Avalokiteśvara’s precious chariot:
with both hands, interlace them facing upward, rotate the jñāna and dhyāna fingers,
and direct the kṣānti and praṇidhi fingers inward.
Recite the mantra three times while visualizing that the Honored One arrives according to one's wish and enters; having thus recited,
[the deity] dwells within the secret heart.
The illusory transformations and floating bubbles ceaselessly arise;
the secret mantra is: Oṃ tura tura hūṃ. Next, bind the eight great lotus mudrās:
first, interlace the two hands.
The powers of progress, generosity, wisdom, and the head [of the deity] support one another;
meditation, aspiration, knowledge, and patience each support one another.
The eight-petaled white lotus opens to the span of one cubit.
Place them upon the vehicle; the mantra of the three secrets is:
Oṃ dūru dūru hūṃ. Next, bind the seal of the eight great lotuses:
join the two wrists together.
The head of the *dāna-prajñā* and the head of the *dhyāna-prajñā* are joined together and held upright, facing upward.
Visualize them as being eight finger-widths apart like precious lotuses,
with their eight petals slightly bent.
The mantra is: Oṃ khaṇḍarohā svāhā. Next, the yoga is explained:
form the secret samaya-mudrā.
Firmly bind [the hands] with the wisdom of *dāna*, joining the *dhyāna* and *prajñā* fingers together and extending them upward.
To awaken this, recite the secret mantra:
Oṃ vajrapadmasamayas tvaṃ. Next, form the Samaya-mudrā for the peace, joy, and delight of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
The ten pāramitās are firmly bound;
patience and aspiration are joined together at the center.
Generosity and wisdom, as well as meditative concentration and knowledge, are joined and held upright.
The mantra is:
Oṃ samaya hūṃ surata-sattvaṃ. Next, perform the mudrā to open the heart-door.
Enter the *vajra-jñāna* syllable and visualize the syllables *tra-la-ta* upon the two breasts.
Like the door-panels of an empty room,
the supreme vajra three-karma simultaneously issues forth the two characters "Fa" (發) and "Zhi" (指), which open the mind.
The mantra is:
Oṃ vajramandhatraṭ. This refers to the seeds perfumed since beginningless time and the defilements that have been presented.
Now, by means of the seal for summoning transgressions,
I shall gather them together, desiring to crush and shatter the ten firm bonds.
The patience and vow are straight as a needle;
the diligence and power are bent like a hook.
With the mind’s thought, one summons all transgressions.
Visualize those various offenses:
planting hair, nakedness, and black forms;
with the inverted seal, pierce them into the heart.
Having touched [the object], one recites the secret mantra;
because the three karmas are brought into correspondence,
one is able to summon all accumulated sins.
Having recited this invocation,
one then performs the rite of destruction.
The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ sarvabodhisattvanirmāṇasamaya-vajra hūṃ jaḥ. Having thus brought [the deity] into the palms of the hands...
Next, perform the rite of destruction.
Interlace the fingers within the previous mudrā and recite:
"MĀṂ! Bind all sins!"
Extending both hands straight with palms joined,
there is the syllable *traṭ*;
visualize it as a vajra.
Striking one another like the crushing of mountains;
through these words of fury and wrathful forms,
one can purify all evil realms.
Having recited [the mantra], one should clasp hands with patience and aspiration.
For twenty-one days, as appropriate,
one should universally summon all sentient beings through compassion and cause them to enter into the removal of all defilements.
Visualize the destruction of all Māras; everything is eliminated and purified like the full moon.
One should visualize an eight-petaled lotus within the heart, with the two elbows joined together.
Upright and facing upward like a precious lotus, with the ten fingers spaced slightly apart and the eight petals of the lotus slightly bent; the secret mantra says:
By means of this gateway of correspondence, through the skillful means of the Buddhas of the past.
The sins accumulated through the three karmas, And immeasurable, most heavy obstructions—
Having utterly destroyed these, they are like fire consuming dry grass.
Sentient beings are perpetually deluded and confused, Failing to understand this profound principle.
Out of the Tathāgata’s great compassion, he opens this secret and wondrous gate.
Next, one should enter the mudrā-binding:
with the two hands firmly bound in the inner *tathāgata-jñāna* syllable, the *dhyāna* and *jñāna* fingers enter within.
With the two powers of progress, they support one another like the shape of a ring.
Visualize an eight-petaled lotus before you; upon it is placed the syllable *vaḥ*, adorned with three dots.
Only then is it rightly called the "Excellence" (*māyā*).
The color is white like a conch or snow; visualize it radiating a thousand rays of light.
By means of the power of progress, form the syllable with the fingers and place it within the heart.
Employing the three karmas in unison, recite this secret mantra.
Once one intends to enter the mind, one should imagine it as radiant light;
this is the very essence of the Dharma-realm.
The practitioner should contemplate this without distinction, awakening to its tranquil purity, for dharmas are fundamentally unarisen.
The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time, through the vajra body, speech, and mind,
employ wondrous skillful means to hold [the essence] within the vajra scroll;
by thus closing the gates of the mind, one attains firmness through the syllable Jñāna.
Then, bending the forefinger and the middle finger, support them against the back of the ring finger and the little finger;
having touched the chest with this seal, recite these sublime words:
Oṃ vajramuṣṭi hūṃ. Next, bind the seal for closing the heart-gate of all Buddhas, the Vajra-seal.
Then, with the eight fingers interlaced,
beginning from the right and turning back,
one moves the left hand three times to and fro against the door leaf.
Visualize the opening of the heart-gate.
The sublime words of the three mysteries are as follows:
Oṃ bhaṇmaduḥpe. Next, perform the mudrā for binding and expelling to demarcate the boundary:
place both hands at the heart, join the fingers of the two hands, and with the right hand, press down upon the left.
Externally, interlace the *kṣānti* (ring) and *vara* (little finger) fingers to form a banner-like shape.
Next, hook the *vīrya* (middle finger) and *bala* (forefinger) fingers with the *śīla* (index finger) square.
Then, join the *dhyāna*, *prajñā*, and *dāna* (thumb) fingers together.
The mantra is:
Oṃ amṛtodbhava hūṃ phaṭ. For one who performs this rite, the Great Compassionate Avalokiteśvara transforms into Hayagrīva Vidyārāja.
Bestowing empowerment upon the practitioner,
once they have swiftly attained Buddhahood, they perform this boundary-binding;
turning three times to the left, they expel all that is unwholesome.
Circumambulate three times to the right,
extending the boundary as far as desired.
Next, having performed the empowerment through the mudrā, visualize the true form by arranging the seed-syllables.
One should visualize the seal-imprint of Avalokiteśvara, with the syllable *hrīḥ* clearly manifest;
this syllable must appear everywhere within the lunar disc,
from which white light radiates from the ūrṇā-kośa, and then gradually withdraws back again.
The two palms join at the heart; the ten fingers interlace within, with the thumbs extended straight upward.
The mudrā is placed upon the crown and the forehead;
first, it covers the two eyes, then the two shoulders, the heart, and the navel.
From the knees to the left shoulder, recite this secret mantra:
*Oṃ āḥ hūṃ svāhā*. Next, form the mudrā and bind it upon one's own body.
Then, visualize oneself as being like the Great Compassionate Avalokiteśvara.
The Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics,
his body of purple-gold color, and his perfect radiance—
having thus bestowed such signs upon him through the Tathāgata’s empowerment.
Touch the crown of the head with the hand-seal and arrange the syllable Oṃ;
touch the forehead and arrange the syllable Ā;
touch the eyes and arrange the syllable Lu.
To the right, following the sequence of the two upper syllables down to the two feet,
one should apply them all by means of tactile placement.
One should imagine *Oṃ* placed upon the head, its color white like the moon.
Emitting immeasurable light, he extinguishes all obstacles;
he is then identical to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
He places his hand upon the crown of this person’s head and rests it upon their forehead; its color becomes entirely golden.
To illuminate all ignorance and darkness, it can produce the light of profound wisdom.
Placed upon the two eyes, its color is like deep lapis lazuli;
it can manifest all forms and characteristics, gradually perfecting the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
Visualize the syllable *Bala* on both shoulders;
its color is like pure white, and because the mind is thus purified, one swiftly reaches the path to Bodhi.
*Svāhā*: visualize the syllable *An* at the navel; its form is red in color.
If one can constantly contemplate this syllable *ha*, one will swiftly attain the turning of the wheel of Dharma.
By placing the syllable *ha* upon the two feet, its color like that of the full moon,
and the practitioner forming this visualization, one will swiftly reach parinirvāṇa.
Visualizing the arrangement of these syllables as golden in color, one immediately accomplishes the supreme Dharma-gate of Great Compassion;
it is also called the true form of the Honored One (Bhagavat). It can extinguish all sins and bring about auspiciousness, being like a mass of vajras, firm and solid.
This is named the supreme and most excellent Dharma of Great Compassion.
If one constantly practices in this manner, it should be known that such a person will swiftly attain *siddhi*.
Having recited the purification mantra three times, one should, with sovereign mastery,
visualize the thousand eyes within the mouth of Avalokiteśvara’s great compassion.
The sublime words and syllables of great compassion emerge and emit five-colored light rays that enter the practitioner’s mouth and are arranged,
circling clockwise within the moon disc of one's own heart.
Then, recite the mantra of the tutelary deity once.
With the ring finger of the right hand, grasp one bead;
when it has passed through the circle, begin again.
Neither too hurried nor too slow, one must not raise the voice.
One must clearly pronounce each syllable so that it can be heard by oneself.
While visualizing the principal deity and the syllables arrayed upon the body, one should perform the recitation and keep count.
Within a single moment of thought, one must simultaneously observe and see [the object];
one must not allow the mind to become distracted by closing the eyes.
If the visualization becomes fatiguing, perform the recitation according to one's strength.
Whether it be one hundred, two hundred, three hundred, or even four hundred up to one thousand recitations,
one should always take a fixed number as the standard.
Even if there are circumstances that require one's presence elsewhere, one must not reduce the number of recitations.
When it reaches one hundred and eight [recitations] or fewer,
this is called "vocal recitation.
If one seeks liberation and wishes to swiftly transcend birth and death, [this is the method].
When performing this yoga of samādhi visualization,
for one whose thoughts are indeterminate and beyond calculation,
their own mind is like the full moon.
It is profoundly serene and pure, with the internal and external clearly distinguished.
Place the syllable *Oṃ* at the center of the moon.

Then, from the front, rotate clockwise to sequentially arrange the syllables *Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā* along the rim of the wheel; contemplate each syllable’s meaning with intense clarity, ensuring it accords with the mind without any discrepancy.
This explains the meaning of the visualization of syllables within *samādhi*.
Regarding the single-syllable gateway "Oṃ," it signifies the flow [of phenomena] that is neither arising nor ceasing.
Furthermore, it is the most supreme meaning among all phenomena.
Regarding the letter-gateway "A," it refers to the *ācārya*.
Having performed the ritual recitation with the Vajra-mudrā according to the Dharma for the sake of the disciple,
and having already conferred the empowerment, one should bestow the Heart-dhāraṇī and cause them to bind the secret mudrā:
by means of the Vajra-bond, join the two thumbs and ring fingers, and bend their upper joints.
Having scattered the flowers from the seal above as an offering,
one should then say:
"This dharma-gate of the mind is the essential secret of all Tathāgatas."
Be careful not to speak of this lightly to others;
it would destroy your samaya. I shall now proclaim its meaning for you.
Listen well now and reflect upon it with close attention.
The syllable A signifies the meaning of non-arising;
it also signifies the meaning of the tranquil wisdom of all Tathāgatas.
As for the gateway of the syllable Lu:
Regarding all phenomena, it has the meaning of non-activity;
furthermore, within the teachings of all Tathāgatas, it has the meaning of neither arising nor abiding.
As for the gateway of the letter *bala*:
The meaning of the peerless awakening of all Tathāgatas is also the meaning of non-abiding,
non-departure, and neither taking nor abandoning.
As for the syllable-gateway *Sva*:
This is the meaning of all Tathāgatas as being peerless and beyond verbal expression.
The letter A-gate is the meaning of the quiescent,
non-abiding nirvāṇa of all Tathāgatas, which is without cause.
Regarding the meanings of the words spoken:
although characters and texts are established, they all possess the meaning of being without characters or texts.
Since there are no characters or texts, one must carefully contemplate each and every aspect of their meaning.
Cycling through and beginning again, it is unrecorded and incalculable, never to be severed.
That which is not severed refers to the most supreme meaning: the continuous flow that is neither born nor extinguished.
Because of the meaning of non-arising and non-ceasing, there is no activity.
Because of the meaning of activity, there is no characteristic.
Because of the meaning of no characteristic, there is no arising or abiding.
Because there is no meaning of arising or abiding, there is no equal enlightenment;
because there is no meaning of equal enlightenment, there is no grasping or abandoning;
because there is no meaning of grasping or abandoning, there is the discourse of equality.
Since the meaning of equality is beyond verbal expression, it is therefore causeless, quiescent, and non-abiding nirvāṇa;
this constitutes the meaning of quiescent, non-abiding nirvāṇa.
Therefore, it is unborn, undying, supreme, and uninterrupted.
This completes the cycle and begins again.
This is called the Mahāyāna Sādhana Method for the Sequence of Samādhi Recitation.
Next, bind the samādhi mudrā.
The two hands are turned upward with the fingers interlaced;
the thumbs are placed back-to-back.
Then, the *dhyāna* and *jñāna* fingers (the index fingers) are held upright, their tips pinching the heads of the thumbs, and the hands are placed upon the crossed legs.
Next, the practitioner should cultivate the āśvāsapraśvāsa-samādhi (the samādhi of inhalation and exhalation).
Sitting upright with the body straight, one should not allow the body to waver.
Pressing the tongue against the upper palate, one should bring the inhalations and exhalations to a state of subtle refinement.
Contemplate with discernment that all phenomena arise from the mind;
all afflictions, secondary afflictions, aggregates, elements, and sense bases are like illusions,
mirages, and cities of the Gandharvas.
Like a whirling firebrand,
like an echo in a valley;
having contemplated in this way, one does not perceive body or mind.
Abiding in the equality of quiescence and signlessness,
taking this as the ultimate wisdom of reality,
one then beholds countless Buddhas within the sky.
It was as if the great earth were filled with sesame seeds;
they all extended their golden arms,
snapped their fingers to rouse him, and spoke these words:
"Son of good family, regarding the state you have realized—
a single path of purity— do not be content until you have realized the vajra-like samādhi or the wisdom of omniscience (sarvajñajñāna)."
"Samantabhadra shall attain supreme perfect enlightenment through fulfillment.
Having heard this exhortation,
the practitioner prostrates to the feet of all Buddhas within meditative concentration.
"I only pray that all Tathāgatas will show me the place where I should practice.
All the Buddhas spoke with one voice, saying:
"You should observe your own mind. Having heard this instruction, he observed his own mind as taught;
after dwelling long in earnest contemplation, he did not perceive any characteristic of his own mind.
He then again visualized prostrating at the Buddha's feet.
He himself declares, "I am the most supreme and honored one. "I do not see my own mind;
what is the characteristic of this mind? All Buddhas inform him that the characteristic of the mind is difficult to fathom, And they bestow upon him the mantra of the mind.
Contemplate with correct reasoning the syllable Oṃ, *samādhi-praṇidhi-hṛdaya*, while clearly perceiving each inhalation and exhalation.
Visualize immeasurable Buddhas within the expanse of space.
At that time, snapping his fingers to alert the practitioner, he addressed him, saying:
"How can you now achieve unexcelled enlightenment?
You do not know the essential Dharma of the true reality of all Buddhas."
At that time, having been awakened,
the practitioner addressed the Buddha,
saying: "What is called 'reality'?"
"I only pray that the Tathāgata will grant me liberation.
At that time, the Buddhas said to the practitioner:
"Excellent, excellent! It is well that you are able to ask such a question."
Visualize the syllable *Āḥ* within your heart;
let it shine with translucent clarity.
The secret mantra is as follows:
Recite "Oṃ cit-ta-prati-vimoka-lu-mi-dhaṃ" once in silence.
Then, visualize a lunar disc as if it were amidst a light mist.
Desiring to bring the lunar disk to purity, in an instant he beholds the mind as perfectly full like the full moon;
he then further reflects: "What is this mind?"
The seeds of the habitual tendencies of affliction—both good and evil—arise from the mind;
the mind is the ālayavijñāna. By taking the cultivation of purity as the cause and through the perfuming of the six perfections, that mind becomes the Great Mind.
The storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is fundamentally non-defiled;
Pure and free from impurity for a long time, it has accumulated merit and wisdom. It is likened to the pure, full moon:
having no substance and no objective reality, Even when spoken of, it is not the moon.
By virtue of possessing merit and wisdom, my own mind is like the full moon;
with a leaping heart, I am filled with joy. Again, I address the World-Honored Ones:
"I have seen my own mind, pure as the full moon."
Free from the stains of all afflictions, such as the grasping of a self and what is grasped—thus have all Buddhas declared:
"Your mind is primordially thus, merely obscured by adventitious dust; through the bodhicitta, it is purified."
Observe the pure lunar disc; having attained the realization of the bodhicitta, receive this heart-mantra. Recite it secretly while contemplating:
Oṃ, I am the nature of the awakened mind (bodhicittasvabhāvātmako ’ham). Reciting this, contemplate the moon of the mind with focused observation.
Make it utterly pure, like the vast expanse of space, free from all blemish or obscuration.
Then, within that moon, visualize a lotus flower;
this shall cause the lunar disk of the mind to become perfectly full and entirely radiant.
The Buddhas spoke again: "Awakening is firm;
one should dwell securely in that firmness. Then they bestowed the heart-mantra:
Oṃ tiṣṭha vajrapadma. One should visualize the lotus and the moon gradually [appearing].
Then, extend [the visualization] so that its measure pervades the entire dharma-realm, equal to space.
Within the pure lunar disc, you should contemplate the five wisdom-vajras,
causing them to universally pervade the dharma-realm as a single great vajra.
One should know that one's own body is the Vajradhātu. Oṃ sarvavajrapadma. Within the lotus.
He emits immeasurable light, from which flow forth infinite and boundless worlds of Ultimate Bliss.
Each world is adorned with exquisite jewels,
and in each there resides a Tathāgata named King Avalokiteśvara.
Surrounded by the assembly of noble ones before and behind;
having contemplated thus, one gradually withdraws the lotus to realize the purity of the mind.
Seeing oneself as a Buddha,
with all marks perfectly complete, One immediately realizes the Samantabhadra Wisdom;
within this samādhi, one universally pays homage to the Buddhas, Praying that they grant empowerment so that [this realization] may be firm and steadfast.
When all the Buddhas had heard the words of the Vajradhātu,
they entered entirely into the vajra and then spoke the mantra of the Vajra-mind, saying:
Oṃ saṃhara pratama. Thus, all the Buddhas and Tathāgatas of all worlds, following the lotus, contract in size until they are equal to their own original bodies;
they then transform their form-bodies into Amitāyus Buddha.
With a body the color of red lapis lazuli, emitting great radiance,
the Buddhas of Great Renown, as soon as they had uttered this vidyā-mantra,
realized the wisdom of reality within the Vajradhātu.
Then those Tathāgatas, having firmly empowered [him], emerged once more from the vajra and dwelt everywhere throughout space.
The practitioner thought: "I have realized the vajra-samādhi."
One shall then possess *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge); in order to bring about the realization of the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) and to cause me to attain perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*),
one should bind the Vajrasamaya-mudrā.
Using the vajra-lotus seat, the practitioner visualizes themselves as the Tathāgata;
fearing further distraction or regression, they next perform the empowerment of the secret mudrā:
interlace the six fingers of the *kṣānti* and *praṇidhāna* hands with their outer fingers crossed.
The two feet advance with power like pillars of lotus; meditation and wisdom are erected together, visualized as a banner.
At the heart, forehead, throat, and crown, recite each mantra once to perform the empowerment.
Following this, perform the mudrā for the sublime invitation. Visualize the syllable *Vṛ* (𭋴哩) at these two [locations].
The mantra says:
"Visualize all the Tathāgatas of space holding the jewel of space and pouring it upon my crown.
With the union of concentration and wisdom, perform the vajra-bond; with the thumbs and ring fingers in the shape of a jewel."
Having performed the empowerment upon the forehead with the mudrā, place the crown of the five buddhas’ wisdom upon the head.
The mantra is: Oṃ prajñārātnābhiṣeke svam hiri trūḥ. Next, bind the flower-garland mudrā.
First, place the two hands at the heart.
Bend the *dhyāna* (middle) and *prajñā* (ring) fingers into the palms.
Form fists with the *kṣānti* (forefinger) and *praṇidhāna* (little finger) as the six *pāramitās*.
From the forehead, extend the fingers like feathers around to the back of the head;
form the lotus-fist in the manner of tying a flower garland.
Slowly move forward and disperse it downward,
visualizing it in the manner of a white sash.
The secret mantra:
Oṃ *praṇamāratnamāle* (with the *ma* pronounced with a retroflex *ṇ*). Next, form the seal of the armor of universal loving-kindness.
Second, firmly fix wisdom at the heart.
The side of the *jina* (victory) power intersects with it.
On the face of the *jina*, one visualizes the syllable Oṃ;
on the face of the power, one visualizes the syllable Ṇa, which is like a central pillar.
It emits green light,
which continues without interruption like drawing lotus fibers.
Once the mind is settled within this, [the practice is complete].
Forming the Wisdom Fist Garland,
once it has been placed behind the forehead, it is then extended forward and downward;
Oṃ, the two hammers are entwined together without interruption.
The green light is like fastened armor.
It proceeds from the heart, back, navel, waist, and above the knees, to the chest, back, throat, neck, and the area behind the forehead;
at each point, it advances with force, circling three times before dispersing.
With celestial robes hanging down before his palms,
he is able to universally protect all sentient beings;
no celestial Māras whatsoever can destroy him.
Recite this mantra:
Oṃ apāyapraśama-karī pūrṇadharakṣaṃ hūṃ haḥ. Next, form the mudrā of the Tathāgata’s Joy.
Place the two wings of concentration and wisdom at the heart;
join the eight fingers of the effort-fingers and cross them outwardly;
place the two fingers of dhyāna and wisdom upright at the heart.
Clapping the hands twice,
he addressed all the holy ones and the assembly of devas:
"With joy, recite this mantra."
It is said:

"Oṃ padma-dūty-āh. Next, the practitioner should, by means of the samādhi of the Wisdom of Accomplishment (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), visualize before his own body a great Lotus King emerging from an inexhaustible ocean.
The stem is made of vajra, its circumference equaling the entire dharma-realm;
above it, one visualizes a pavilion of seven treasures,
wherein upon a lion throne is a pure full moon.
Within it appears a wondrous white lotus flower.
One contemplates the gateway of the syllable *sa*,
emitting great radiance that universally illumines the entire dharma-realm.
Having contemplated the Great Compassion of Avalokiteśvara,
one further contemplates before oneself the Land of Peace and Bliss,
with its ground of lapis lazuli and its ocean of merit-milk.
Within that ocean, one visualizes the syllable Kṛm;
it transforms into subtle, blossoming lotuses,
which then transform into the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvararāja.
His physical marks are majestic and adorned; his body color is like that of the Tathāgata Padmaprabha, resembling the moon.
Upon his head he wears a crown of the five Tathāgatas, and he drapes exquisite celestial garments of fine silk.
Adorned with necklaces, his body radiated light everywhere;
he was surrounded by an immeasurable and incalculable assembly of great bodhisattvas as his retinue.
The practitioner, desiring to cause all Tathāgatas to assemble,
next employs the Vajrarāja Bodhisattva Samādhi to summon the assembly of noble ones.
Next, bind the Lotus Hook-Summoning Mudrā:
with the two hands of Samādhi and Prajñā forming vajra-fists,
extend the forefingers like hooks and bend only the third joints.
Recite this secret mantra:
Oṃ padma-kūṣmāṇḍa hūṃ jaḥ. Recite this three times and perform three prostrations with joined palms.
The Bodhisattva of the True Body shall arrive as soon as he is called to mind.
Next, bind the Great Seal of the Vajra Lasso.
Introduce the honored body into the essence of wisdom.
Interlace the hands externally for the six perfections of patience and aspiration;
support the two fingers of meditation and diligence against one another.
Recite this mantra:
Oṃ padmamoghapāśa hūṃ. [Thus] the Dharma-body of the Bodhisattva enters the painted image.
Next, perform the vajra-śṛṅkhalā mudrā.
It causes the deity to abide firmly;
through the union of meditative concentration, diligence, power,
and wisdom, this is called the Vajra-Śamana-mudrā.
Recite this secret mantra:
Oṃ padma saṃpāta hūṃ. Having performed this rite, the holy one’s own form remains empowered without dispersing.
Next, bind the seal of the Vajra Wondrous Bell,
which can cause all the sages to rejoice:
bend the wisdom fingers into the vajra-bond.
Bend the tips of the forefingers inward so they touch like a ring;
this is called the Vajra-ānanda-mudrā.
Recite this mantra:
Oṃ padmaveśa hūṃ. By performing this rite,
all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and original holy ones will be entirely delighted.
Next, bind the mudrā of the Argha-water dhāraṇī.
Take saffron, camphor, and white sandalwood, mix them with scented water in an argha vessel,
and offer it while holding it aloft.
Next, perform the arghya mudrā:
join both hands at the heart;
extend the six fingers of the *kṣānti* and *praṇidhāna* [fingers] upward and straight.
Exerting one's strength, one should don the armor of dhyāna and prajñā and recite this secret mantra:
Oṃ tatre buddhāya svāhā. One who performs this offering...
Just as one sprinkles the vajra-amṛta of all Tathāgatas upon the crowns of the heads of all sentient beings,
thereby eliminating the immeasurable karmic obstructions of those beings.
Those who drink this water shall be freed from all calamities and afflictions.
By means of the consecration of the *argha* offering,
one should hold up the various fragrant waters for the *argha*.
Visualize bathing the stainless bodies of all the noble ones;
you shall thereby attain the stage of the Dharma-Cloud of Empowerment (*abhiṣeka-dharmameghā-bhūmi*).
Next, form the seal of the hundred-syllable *dhāraṇī* of all Tathāgatas by firmly binding the ten fingers.
With meditative concentration and wisdom held upright together,
the secret mantra says:

Oṃ *praṇamya* sarvasattvasamayamanupālaya *praṇamya* sattva-tvayi-nopatiṣṭha jvalatu tejo me bhava anurakṣa me bhava subhāṣitena me bhava saṃśrīdāṃ me prayaccha sarvakarma-sucayaṃ gṛhṇa śrīyoga-kuru hūṃ ha ha ha ha hoḥ bhagavan sarvatathāgata-praṇama-maṃ mañjuśe praṇame bhava mahāsamayasattva-ayomi-mahāyantra. By means of the empowerment of this hundred-syllable mantra.
Even if one has committed the five crimes of immediate retribution,
slandered all Buddhas and the Vaipulya sutras, or practiced mantra,
by virtue of the fact that the deity remains firmly established within one's own body, [one shall be purified].
All siddhis sought in the present life,
namely the most supreme siddhi and the siddhi of Vajrasattva.
Up to the supreme siddhi of the Tathāgata,
one next binds the Vajralāsyā mudrā to accomplish the inner retinue of the Tathāgata.
The union of samādhi and prajñā is the vajra;
the two fingers of dhyāna and prajñā are held upright at the heart.
This is the stage for all playful discourse.
Visualize the wheel-mudrā at the crown of the head according to the sacred intent.
Recite this mantra:
Oṃ padmalakṣye hūḥ. For one who performs this rite:
Just as one makes offerings to all Buddhas with the wisdom of all Tathāgatas to cultivate joy,
so too does one do so by means of playful sport as an offering.
Before long, one shall realize the Vajra Samādhi.
Next, bind the Vajra Flower Garland Mudrā and visualize the universal Dharma-realm as a sublime cloud of garlands.
Without altering the previous mudrā, hold it forward.
Visualize holding a precious garland to adorn and protect [the deity].
Recite this mantra:
Oṃ pramamale traṭ. One who performs this rite is as if making an offering with a garland of bodhi flowers.
By making an offering with the vajra-garland,
one shall be conferred the position of the Dharma King through the rite of empowerment.
Next, one should bind the mudrā of the vajra-song.
I praise the Tathāgata’s merit and wisdom;
contemplating his marks and signs, he utters a pure sound,
thereby accords with the principle of suchness.
Is this not the Vajra Song and Praise Mudrā,
which extols the Buddha’s wisdom with sublime sounds?
The previous mudrā is released from the navel up to the mouth.
Producing exquisite musical sounds to delight the assembly of sages, he recites this mantra:
Oṃ padma nīti nījaḥ. For one who performs this rite:
If one makes offerings by chanting with the secret mantras of all Tathāgatas,
before long one shall possess the eloquence of a Tathāgata.
Next, one should bind the sublime mudrā of the Vajra Dance.
Visualizing the wondrous celestial maidens making universal offerings,
the two wings of concentration and wisdom each perform a swirling dance;
[they move] to the right flank, the left flank, and again to the center of the chest.
Each time one advances, circle [the deity] three times;
gradually reciting the mantra, scatter it above the crown of the head.
Recite this sublime mantra as follows:
Oṃ pramāṇiti kṛta. One who performs this rite is as if making an offering with the eloquence of all the Tathāgatas.
By means of offering exquisite dance,
one shall attain the mind-born body (manomayakāya) of a Tathāgata.
Next, perform the external offering of burning incense by forming the mudrā.
This universally perfumes the ocean-like assembly of Buddhas;
the hands are joined at the vajra level and then opened downward,
visualizing clouds of sublime fragrance pervading the entire dharma-realm.
Recite this mantra:
Oṃ padmadhūpe hūṃ. For one who performs this rite, it is as if all the exquisite incenses of the world were being burned as an offering.
It enables all sentient beings to attain pure fruits,
by virtue of making offerings of incense.
One immediately attains the wondrous, unimpeded wisdom.
Next, bind the Vajra Flower-scattering mudrā;
with this, adorn all world-systems.
The binding mudrā is released upward like scattering playful flowers;
fragrant clouds of blossoms pervade the entire dharma realm.
Recite this mantra as follows:
Oṃ padma puṣpe. One who performs this rite shall likewise offer all manner of exquisite worldly flowers as an offering;
this will enable sentient beings to swiftly attain accomplishment and become endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Tathāgata.
By binding the vajra-flower mudrā of offering,
one swiftly realizes the thirty-two marks of a Tathāgata.
Next, bind the vajra-lamp mudrā.
The hands of Samantaprabhā illuminate the Buddha’s assembly with radiant light;
the fingers of the patience and vow mudrās are interlaced externally,
while the fingers of vigor and power are bent and supported to form the shape of a jewel.
With meditative concentration and wisdom pressing forward, one performs the vajra-bind;
the light of the maṇi-lamp illuminates the dharma-realm.
Recite this mantra:
Oṃ *praṇamāmi*— one who performs this rite thereby makes an offering with the wisdom-lamp of all the Tathāgatas.
It enables sentient beings to swiftly achieve the wisdom of the Tathāgata;
by making offerings of vajra-lamps,
they quickly become endowed with the five eyes of the Tathāgata.
Next, bind the vajra-unguent mudrā.
Use it to make offerings to the assembly of all Buddhas;
scatter the vajra-bind as if with unguent.
The fragrance circulates throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
The mantra is:
Oṃ padma-ghaṇṭe svāhā. For one who performs this rite:
Just as one makes an offering with the fragrance of the ethical discipline (*śīla*) of the wisdom of all Tathāgatas,
which enables all sentient beings to swiftly attain the body of pure ethical discipline,
so too does one do so by binding the Vajra Incense Mudrā.
One attains the wisdom of the fivefold Dharma-body.
Having thus extensively performed the Buddha-activities,
one should next perform recitation while observing with clear attention.
First, one should single-mindedly visualize the deity.
Through the four vidyās, the deity is drawn into one's own body;
the wisdom-body and the deity are non-dual.
His physical form and majestic deportment are equal [to those of the Buddhas],
surrounded by a retinue of assemblies;
he abides in the Great Mirror-like Wisdom of Parinirvāṇa.
Form the vajra-bind with the two wings of concentration and wisdom;
erect the two fingers of the patience and wish-fulfillment mudrās like banners,
and then recite the root mantra of Avalokiteśvara.
Visualize yourself as a *sattva* within a moon disc and recite this mantra:
Oṃ ekalokeśvara rājā hṛdaya. Next, the *dhāraṇī* for the Great, Vast, Perfect, Unobstructed Compassionate Heart is taught: Oṃ maṇi padme hūṃ | tadyathā | gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā.

Having recited the root mantra seven times while holding the rosary,
one should bring it to the crown of the head;
then, remaining firmly established in meditative equipoise with the mind focused at the heart, one should perform the recitation.
With the tip of the tongue slightly moving and the lips and teeth joined,
one contemplates the physical marks and signs of the body in both forward and reverse order.
One should diligently practice these at all four times of the day without interruption, setting a limit of no fewer than a thousand or a hundred repetitions.
Furthermore, surpassing all supernatural powers as well as merit and wisdom,
one becomes equal in this very life to the Honored One Samantabhadra.
Once the practitioner has completed the allotted duration of recitation, [they should proceed].
Holding the jewel upon the crown of the head, one should diligently make the great vow;
thereafter, forming the samādhi mudrā,
one enters the dharmadhātu-svabhāva-samādhi.
Cultivate the *Akṣaraparivarta-dhāraṇī*:
All phenomena are fundamentally unarisen; their intrinsic nature transcends verbal expression, being pure and free from defilement, equal to space by reason of karma and so forth.
Turning back and reflecting with careful attention, In every syllable one awakens to the reality;
Though there are differences between the beginning and the end, That which is realized all returns to the One.
Without abandoning this samādhi, One possesses non-abiding, objectless compassion.
May all sentient beings universally aspire to be no different from me.
The practitioner emerges from samādhi,
then forms the root mudrā and recites the root mantra seven times.
Furthermore, regarding the great offering:
the Buddha, with wondrous sounds and words, extols and praises [the deity] and offers argha water;
then, by means of the seal for subduing the three times, he releases the boundary by rotating it to the right.
Form the Vajra Liberation Mudrā.
Send off the various holy ones as before, performing repentance;
then address the Honored One himself.
Having completed the generation of the aspiration,
next perform the seal of dismissal.
Disperse the previously mentioned root seal from the navel up to the face.
Placing one's palms together at the crown of the head,
one should visualize the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvararāja; then,
returning to one's own palace, one should recite this mantra.

"Oṃ vajrapadma muḥ. Having thus dispatched the *iṣṭadevatā*, make aspirations as you wish, and then again employ the armor mudrā (*kavaca-mudrā*).
To protect the body, first perform the boundary-binding mudrā of Hayagrīva;
then, releasing the boundaries by rotating them counter-clockwise, proceed to walk about as you wish.
Go to a secluded place and prepare offerings of incense and flowers.
Recite and chant Mahāyāna sūtras such as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, *Avataṃsaka*, *Nirvāṇa*, and *Laṅkāvatāra*.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, constantly maintain mindfulness of the Honored One without interruption.
If there are sentient beings who encounter this teaching and practice it with diligence throughout the four periods of day and night,
they will realize the Stage of Joy in their present life.
In the sixteenth kalpa thereafter, he will attain perfect enlightenment.
That which has been translated above is a brief summary of this dhāraṇī, spoken in accordance with what was previously explained.
Each and every syllable contains within it the eighty thousand *sūtra* treasuries and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of *dhāraṇī* gates of revolving;
each and every gate expounds the profound *tathatā* and the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
For this reason, throughout successive dynasties, those who have translated and transmitted these texts have rarely been able to explain them;
moreover, because they did not understand their meaning,
they all received the same protective empowerment and thus collectively referred to them as "mantras" (dhāraṇīs).
Is this not truly lamentable?
It is said that *dhāraṇī* is sometimes called *mantra*,
and sometimes called *vidyārāja*.
There are many such designations;
to simply call them "spells" (zhòu) is no different from calling them "curses" (zhǒuzhù). What distinction is there between the two?
This, then, is an error in the translation.
Furthermore, as for those who claim it is a "transmission," do they expect to be without fault?
